entries.name: GPU Accelerated Compute
entries.thesisShort: NVIDIA still supplies roughly 80-88% of the AI accelerator market. Data center revenue set a record $89.0B in Q2 FY2027, up 117% year over year on the Blackwell Ultra ramp, with Vera Rubin shipping behind it and the October quarter guided to $108B as big-four hyperscaler capex steps up about 77% to roughly $725B in 2026.
entries.thesisLong:
NVIDIA's chokehold on accelerated compute is the single most important bottleneck in the AI stack. Hopper gave way to Blackwell (B200/GB200 NVL72), then Blackwell Ultra (B300), and Vera Rubin moved into a full production ramp announced at GTC Taipei on 1 June 2026. The VR200 carries 288GB of HBM4 at 22 TB/s and roughly 50 PFLOPS of FP4 compute, about 3.3x the throughput of B300. Each generation has been allocation-constrained rather than demand-constrained: Rubin began shipping in Q3 2026 with the volume ramp in Q4 2026, and early supply is being routed to hyperscalers and frontier labs first while Blackwell Ultra carries current revenue.

The moat is not just silicon. CUDA, NCCL, TensorRT-LLM, and the Mellanox/NVLink fabric form a software-plus-network stack that competitors cannot replicate in a single product cycle. Every serious foundation model lab — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, xAI — runs production training on NVIDIA, and inference is following the same path.

The demand backdrop is the capex cycle underneath it. Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta together plan roughly $725B of capital spending in 2026, up about 77% year over year, with roughly three-quarters of it AI-related. NVIDIA data center revenue reached a record $89.0B in the July 2026 quarter, up 117% year over year and 18% sequentially, on total revenue of $96.2B; the company guided the October quarter to $108B. Sovereign AI deals (Saudi Humain, UAE G42, Japan, France) add a second demand vector independent of US hyperscalers.

The pressure on the moat is now measurable rather than theoretical. TrendForce expects custom ASIC shipments to grow about 44.6% in 2026 against 16.1% for merchant GPUs, and Broadcom alone has booked multi-gigawatt XPU programs with Google, Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta. HBM4 supply and advanced-packaging capacity also physically cap how many Rubin racks can be built in 2026-2027. But on the bottleneck question — who gates AI compute supply in 2026 — the answer remains NVIDIA.

entries.name: Custom AI Silicon & Networking
entries.thesisShort: Broadcom is the primary second source for hyperscaler AI compute via custom XPUs and supplies the Ethernet switching that fabrics AI clusters; AI semiconductor revenue hit a record $10.8B in Q2 FY2026, up 143% year over year.
entries.thesisLong:
Broadcom occupies a unique seat: it co-designs the custom AI accelerators that hyperscalers use to escape NVIDIA dependency, while simultaneously supplying the Tomahawk and Jericho switching silicon that fabrics every modern AI cluster — including NVIDIA-based ones. That dual exposure keeps Broadcom relevant whether the merchant-GPU path or the custom-silicon path prevails.

The custom-silicon book has moved from speculation to contracted volume. On its Q2 FY2026 call (3 June 2026), Broadcom reported record AI semiconductor revenue of $10.8B, up 143% year over year, and described long-term multi-gigawatt supply arrangements with Google, Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta, with significant new deployments beginning in fiscal 2027. A further $6B of AI orders was booked from two additional customers, including an initial one-gigawatt order covering XPUs and networking that starts delivery in the second half of 2027.

Networking is the second leg and roughly 40% of Q2 FY2026 AI revenue. Tomahawk 6, the industry’s only 100-terabit Ethernet switch, has been shipping for over a year, and the next-generation 200-terabit part taped out during the quarter. As Ethernet displaces InfiniBand outside NVIDIA reference designs, Broadcom switch silicon sits inside most hyperscaler fabrics.

The structural risk is concentration and timing: a handful of customers drive most AI revenue, the largest booked programs do not deliver until 2H 2027, and any hyperscaler bringing networking silicon in-house compresses the moat. But for the next two years, the AI bottleneck story includes Broadcom by necessity.

entries.name: MI-Series Accelerators
entries.thesisShort: AMD remains the only merchant alternative to NVIDIA at scale; data center revenue more than doubled to $6.7B in Q2 2026 as the MI400 and the Helios rack platform entered production, with revenue shipments starting at the end of Q3 2026.
entries.thesisLong:
AMD is the credible number two in merchant AI silicon. MI300X shipped first to Microsoft, Meta and Oracle as inference workhorses; MI325X added HBM3e capacity that favoured memory-bound workloads; MI355X (CDNA4) brought FP4/FP6 datatypes; and at Advancing AI 2026 in San Francisco, Lisa Su unveiled the fully specified MI400 line, the Helios rack platform, and a 2027 MI500 preview. Each MI400 carries 432GB of HBM4, and AMD claims roughly 10x the frontier-model training performance of MI300X.

The financial trajectory has turned sharply. Data center revenue was $5.8B in Q1 2026 (+57% YoY) and $6.7B in Q2 2026 (+107% YoY, +16% sequentially), roughly 58% of total company revenue, driven by both EPYC server processors and the Instinct ramp. Helios entered full production with revenue shipments beginning at the end of Q3 2026, which is the point at which rack-scale AMD systems start competing directly with NVIDIA reference racks rather than at the accelerator level.

The software gap has narrowed materially. PyTorch, vLLM, SGLang and the major inference stacks run cleanly on MI-series, and production Llama inference at Meta is the proof point that the stack is viable for Tier 1 customers at scale.

The bottleneck role is real but secondary: AMD is the hyperscaler hedge against NVIDIA scarcity and pricing, and it is the only merchant supplier pairing leading-edge GPUs with leading-edge server CPUs (Turin, Venice) into a full rack. As long as NVIDIA stays supply-constrained, AMD captures spillover demand. If supply loosens, AMD has to win on price-performance instead.

entries.name: EUV Lithography
entries.thesisShort: ASML is the sole supplier of EUV lithography on the planet, and every leading-edge AI chip — Rubin, MI400, the hyperscaler TPUs — physically cannot exist without an ASML scanner.
entries.thesisLong:
ASML's EUV monopoly is the most durable bottleneck in the entire technology economy. There is no second source. Nikon and Canon abandoned EUV development a decade ago, and the IP plus supply chain (Zeiss optics, Cymer light sources, thousands of component suppliers) is uncopiable inside any reasonable investment horizon. Every leading-edge logic node at TSMC, Samsung and Intel runs on ASML scanners, full stop.

High-NA is now moving from demonstration to qualification. ASML recognised revenue on two High-NA systems in Q4 2025, shipped the first EXE:5200 for high-volume manufacturing, and reached a readiness milestone on the first high-volume logic product with Intel. Intel completed acceptance testing on a second-generation EXE:5200B, SK hynix installed the same system at a DRAM fab, Samsung took delivery of its first scanner in late 2025, and imec is targeting Q4 2026 qualification. The EXE:5200B lists at roughly $380M per tool.

The order book has become harder to read, which is itself part of the story. From Q1 2026 ASML stopped publishing quarterly net bookings; backlog is now effectively an annual disclosure, and the most recent published figure is roughly €38.8B at the end of 2025, of which about €25.5B was EUV. Guidance and management commentary now carry the signal instead. Q2 2026 delivered €9.3B of net sales at a 54.0% gross margin and €2.9B of net income, ahead of guidance on strong Installed Base Management sales, and full-year 2026 revenue guidance was raised to €36-40B.

The risks are concentrated and political: China export controls already blocked EUV and tightened DUV, and further escalation removes addressable market. Cyclicality also matters — each tool is a $200-380M lump. But on the chokepoint question, ASML is the textbook answer: a single Dutch company gates the physical creation of every advanced AI chip.

entries.name: Process Control & Inspection
entries.thesisShort: KLA holds roughly 60% of process control with no competitor above 8%, and it is the de facto standard for EUV defect inspection — every High-NA wafer at TSMC, Samsung and Intel passes through a KLA tool.
entries.thesisLong:
KLA is the unsung monopoly of leading-edge logic. As nodes shrink to 2nm and below, defect detection becomes existential — a single missed particle can kill an entire wafer worth tens of thousands of dollars. KLA's optical and e-beam inspection systems sit at every critical step of the EUV flow, and third-party industry data published in 2026 puts its process control share near 60%, with no competitor above 8%.

The June 2026 quarter (fiscal Q4 2026) was a record: $3.66B of revenue and $1.36B of GAAP net income, with revenue, profitability and EPS all above the midpoint of guidance. Management attributed the strength to AI infrastructure investment, leading-edge foundry/logic demand, and rising process control intensity, and expects the process control systems business to grow more than 20% in 2026 — outpacing a wafer fab equipment market that peers now size in the low $150B range for the calendar year.

The High-NA EUV transition is a particular tailwind. Smaller features mean smaller defects, which means more inspection passes and higher-resolution tools. Advanced packaging adds a second vector as CoWoS capacity expands and hybrid bonding introduces new inspection steps.

Risks are the familiar WFE set: China exposure under export controls, capex cyclicality after an exceptional 2026, and customer concentration at the top logic foundries. But process control is the least substitutable WFE category, and KLA is the least substitutable name in it.

entries.name: Materials Engineering
entries.thesisShort: Applied Materials is the broadest WFE supplier and a leader in deposition for advanced packaging and gate-all-around transistors; fiscal Q3 2026 revenue hit a record $9.1B with the October quarter guided to roughly $10.25B.
entries.thesisLong:
Applied Materials is the swiss-army-knife of semiconductor manufacturing — deposition (CVD, PVD, epi), etch, ion implant, CMP and inspection. No other company has product breadth across this many process steps, which is why Applied benefits from every node transition regardless of whether the bottleneck is logic, memory or packaging.

Fiscal Q3 2026 (reported August 2026) was a record: $9.115B of revenue, up 25% year over year and 15% sequentially, with non-GAAP EPS of $3.50 ahead of consensus. Semiconductor Systems drove the result as orders accelerated across DRAM, leading-edge foundry-logic and advanced packaging, lifting segment non-GAAP operating margin to 38.0%. Management guided the October quarter to roughly $10.25B, up 51% year over year, with non-GAAP EPS of about $4.02.

The gate-all-around transition at TSMC N2, Samsung 2nm and Intel 18A is a meaningful tailwind, since GAA stacks more deposition steps per wafer than FinFET and Applied estimates roughly 20% more WFE intensity per wafer as a result. Advanced packaging is the second growth vector: hybrid bonding tools, through-silicon-via etch and plating systems are core to CoWoS, SoIC and Foveros workflows, and Applied expects leading-edge foundry-logic, DRAM and advanced packaging to drive around 80% of WFE growth across 2026 and 2027.

China remains the structural swing factor. Its share of revenue eased to 28% in the quarter from 35% a year earlier under regulatory constraints, though the CFO expects absolute China revenue to grow this calendar year and next, led by 28nm foundry-logic. Cyclicality and ICAPS normalization are the other risks, but the breadth across nodes, devices and customers makes Applied the most diversified name in the WFE complex.

entries.name: Etch & Deposition for Memory
entries.thesisShort: Lam Research leads etch — the most critical step for 3D NAND scaling and HBM through-silicon vias — and posted $6.72B of revenue in the June 2026 quarter at a 52% gross margin, its highest in twenty years.
entries.thesisLong:
Lam Research is the etch specialist of the WFE world. Third-party estimates of its etch share vary across roughly 45-55% depending on methodology, but in the most demanding applications — high-aspect-ratio dielectric etch for 3D NAND, TSV etch for HBM, and selective etch for gate-all-around — Lam's position is stronger still. As NAND stacks climb and HBM4 demands deeper vias, etch intensity per wafer rises structurally.

The June 2026 quarter showed that leverage: $6.72B of revenue, up 15% sequentially and 30% year over year, at a 52% gross margin — the company's best in two decades. The September 2026 quarter is guided to $8.10B ±$400M with a 39.5% ±1pt operating margin, a step-up that reflects how quickly memory and leading-edge logic orders have converted.

The HBM cycle is the near-term driver. HBM3e and HBM4 require deep silicon vias and precise stack alignment, and Lam platforms are qualified at SK hynix, Samsung and Micron. CEO Tim Archer now expects calendar 2026 wafer fab equipment spending in the low $150B range, raised from a prior view of about $140B with upside bias — a sector-level revision that frames how far the memory build has run ahead of April expectations.

Dry resist development with ASML remains a longer-term call option: if dry resist displaces wet photoresist for EUV, Lam captures a step that previously belonged elsewhere in the flow. The risks are the mirror image of the upside — memory cycle volatility after a record year, China demand normalization, and concentration at the top three memory makers.

entries.name: HBM & High-Performance Memory
entries.thesisShort: Micron is the only US HBM supplier and the third leg of the HBM oligopoly with SK hynix and Samsung; its 2026 HBM supply is sold out under multi-year contracts, with management able to fill only half to two-thirds of customer demand.
entries.thesisLong:
Micron is the only US-headquartered HBM supplier and the third leg of an oligopoly with SK hynix and Samsung. Every NVIDIA Rubin and AMD MI400 accelerator needs this memory to function, which makes HBM allocation — not wafer starts — the binding constraint on how many AI systems can physically be built.

The fiscal Q3 2026 quarter (reported 24 June 2026) showed how tight that constraint has become. Revenue reached roughly $41.5B, several times the year-ago quarter, with gross margin above 81% against 27% a year earlier. CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said Micron can fulfil only between half and two-thirds of customer demand, with the entire 2026 HBM supply sold out under multi-year contracts and both HBM3E and HBM4 fully booked through calendar 2027, with demand extending into 2028.

HBM4 is the swing product. Micron's HBM4 revenue has already passed $1B and the generation is ramping roughly twice as fast as HBM3E. That said, Micron remains third by share among the three HBM suppliers and reportedly holds the thinnest slice of NVIDIA's HBM4 allocation, which is the clearest structural limit on how much of the cycle it captures.

The risks run in the opposite direction to the last two years. Supply additions from SK hynix and Samsung eventually normalize pricing, and a gross margin above 80% is a cyclical peak rather than a run-rate. Idaho and Japan capacity coming online, plus custom HBM base-die programs with hyperscalers, are the offsets that determine how much of this cycle converts into durable share.

entries.name: Leading-Edge Foundry
entries.thesisShort: TSMC fabricates effectively every advanced AI chip on Earth and controls more than 90% of global CoWoS output, and it raised 2026 capex to $60-64B to chase 2nm and advanced packaging demand.
entries.thesisLong:
TSMC fabricates effectively every advanced AI chip on Earth — NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, Apple, the hyperscaler TPUs — and the constraint has shifted from transistors to packaging. Q2 2026 revenue was $40.2B at a 67.7% gross margin, modestly ahead of guidance.

The capex line is where the demand signal is clearest. TSMC raised full-year 2026 capex to $60-64B from a prior $52-56B range, implying second-half spending of $33.2-37.2B, a year-over-year increase of 56-75%. That step-up is a direct response to the 2nm ramp and to advanced packaging, where Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate has become the industry’s most critical bottleneck. TSMC controls more than 90% of global CoWoS output, and monthly capacity of roughly 90,000 wafers is expected to reach about 120,000 by the end of 2026.

The cost of that ramp is visible in the margin outlook. TSMC guided gross margin to 65-67%, below elevated expectations, with 2nm ramp costs the stated cause — the classic pattern where a node transition front-loads depreciation before the pricing benefit arrives. A16 with backside power delivery follows in 2027.

The risks are unchanged in kind and unchanged in weight: Taiwan Strait geopolitical exposure, concentration in a small number of very large customers, rising leading-edge fab costs, and currency translation between the NT dollar and USD.

entries.name: Western Foundry Alternative
entries.thesisShort: Intel Foundry is the only meaningful US-soil leading-edge alternative to TSMC, with 18A now in high-volume internal production — but external foundry revenue was just $293M in Q2 2026 and no 14A anchor customer has been named.
entries.thesisLong:
Intel Foundry is the only meaningful US-soil leading-edge foundry alternative to TSMC, and 2026 is the year the technology case and the commercial case visibly diverged.

On technology, the news is genuinely good. 18A reached high-volume internal production, and in Q2 2026 output exceeded internal targets by roughly 25% and rose more than 50% sequentially, with yields reported near 85% against roughly 90% at TSMC N2. Intel Foundry cut the cost of its primary Panther Lake SKU by roughly 50% year to date and targets a further 20% this year. 18A-P entered risk production, and the 0.9 PDK for Intel 14A is on track for October 2026 after PDK 0.5 completed.

On commerce, the gap is stark. External foundry revenue was $293M in Q2 2026 against a $2.1B Foundry operating loss, and no external 14A anchor customer has been named. Management has said explicitly that 14A capacity will only be developed against firm external commitments — a deliberate break from the previous build-first posture, and the single most important constraint on how large this business can become. A Fortinet agreement broke the customer-disclosure silence ahead of Q2, and Terafab, a reported joint venture involving Tesla, SpaceX and xAI, has been described as planning to use 14A, with firm supplier decisions expected between 2H 2026 and 1H 2027.

So the bottleneck framing holds — the West has exactly one candidate for a second leading-edge source — but the commercial proof is still ahead, and it is gated on the October 2026 PDK and the anchor-customer decisions that follow.

entries.name: Specialty & Trailing-Edge Foundry
entries.thesisShort: GlobalFoundries is the leading Western pure-play on specialty silicon — RF, automotive, silicon photonics and FDX — that the AI infrastructure stack quietly depends on, and it ran fabs in the high-80s% utilization in Q2 2026.
entries.thesisLong:
GlobalFoundries is the leading Western pure-play on specialty silicon — RF, automotive, silicon photonics and FDX — the categories the AI infrastructure stack quietly depends on for power management, optical I/O and networking ASICs. It does not chase leading-edge logic, which caps the multiple but also insulates it from the capex arms race.

Q2 2026 (reported August 2026) showed the AI pivot working through the numbers: revenue of $1.79B and non-IFRS EPS of $0.46, both ahead of consensus, with non-IFRS operating margin of 16.7%, up 140 basis points year over year on improved manufacturing productivity. Management now expects full-year gross margin of about 30%, rather than merely exiting 2026 at that level. Fab utilization ran in the high 80s with roughly 10 points of headroom still available — enough to absorb incremental AI-adjacent demand without a new capex cycle.

The acquisition of Synopsys' Processor IP Solutions — the ARC and MIPS assets — added 150-plus patents, access to 300-plus customers and 400-plus engineers, and is now expected to contribute $100-120M of technology-services revenue in 2026, raised from a prior $60-100M. Those businesses are R&D-intensive but carry gross margins above corporate targets. The company also recognised $675M of government support in the quarter.

The risks are demand-side rather than technology-side: handset and automotive softness, customer concentration, and the structural fact that limited leading-edge participation caps how much of the AI build GlobalFoundries can address.

entries.name: Advanced Packaging OSAT
entries.thesisShort: Amkor is the only US-listed advanced packaging OSAT and now holds a ten-year advanced packaging agreement with TSMC in Arizona plus an NVIDIA packaging and test program — the package-side bottleneck for AI accelerators.
entries.thesisLong:
Amkor is the only US-listed advanced packaging OSAT, and packaging — not lithography — is where AI accelerator supply is currently rationed. Q2 2026 was a record: revenue of $1.90B, up 26% year over year, with growth across all end markets and records in computing, automotive and industrial. Communications sales grew 32%, automotive and industrial 35%, and computing 23%.

The operating leverage finally showed. Gross margin expanded to 16.8%, up 480 basis points year over year, and net income attributable to Amkor rose to $173.8M, or $0.70 per diluted share. Q3 2026 is guided to roughly $2.0B of revenue.

Arizona is the strategic centre of gravity. Phase 1 of the Arizona facility is now fully committed, the company added 67 acres to the campus, and it is preparing further expansion to match customer demand. Two anchor relationships underpin it: a ten-year advanced packaging agreement with TSMC in Arizona, and an NVIDIA arrangement covering advanced packaging and test for next-generation AI infrastructure. That combination converts what was previously CoWoS overflow into contracted, onshore capacity.

The cost is cash. Capital spending of $688.4M in the first half drove free cash flow to negative $269.9M, and the 2026 capex plan remains $2.5-3.0B, most of it aimed at facilities and advanced packaging capacity. Customer concentration and capex absorption if AI packaging demand softens are the live risks.

entries.name: Liquid Cooling & Power Distribution
entries.thesisShort: Vertiv supplies the thermal and power content inside AI reference racks, and raised 2026 guidance to $13.8-14.2B on 30-32% organic growth — though it stopped publishing backlog and order figures with the Q2 2026 release.
entries.thesisLong:
Vertiv sits at the thermal and power layer of the AI rack: liquid cooling, busway, rack PDU and UPS content that ships alongside the accelerators rather than instead of them. Q2 2026 net sales were $3.274B, up $636M or 24% year over year, comprising 18% organic growth, 5% from acquisitions and 1% from favourable currency. Diluted EPS grew 53% and adjusted diluted EPS 60%.

Management raised full-year 2026 guidance across every key metric: net sales of $13.8-14.2B (30-32% organic growth), adjusted operating profit of $3.285-3.365B, adjusted diluted EPS of $6.65-6.75 (58-61% growth), and adjusted free cash flow of $2.4-2.6B.

One disclosure change matters for anyone tracking this as a bottleneck. The Q2 2026 release contained no backlog figure and no orders number at all — a break from prior practice, where the company had reported $8.5B of backlog at Q2 2025. Guidance is now the primary forward signal, and the visibility that made Vertiv legible as a leading indicator for AI rack deployment has narrowed.

The structural position is unchanged: liquid cooling is the default for new AI data center designs, and Vertiv content is specified into reference architectures rather than bid per project. The dependencies are the flip side of that — reliance on the accelerator vendors' reference designs, and exposure to any hyperscaler capex digestion.

chokepointMetrics.value: Not published in the Q2 2026 release (last disclosed: $8.5B at Q2 2025)

Sovereign AI build-outs specifying complete power and cooling systems
Raised 2026 guidance across sales, margin, EPS and free cash flow
Service revenue compounding with the installed base
risks: Backlog and orders no longer disclosed quarterly, reducing forward visibility
Dependence on accelerator-vendor reference designs
Hyperscaler capex digestion

entries.name: Electrical Infrastructure
entries.thesisShort: Eaton is the largest US supplier of the medium-voltage switchgear, busway and PDUs that move power from substation to GPU; data center orders rose roughly 240% year over year in Q2 2026 against a 307 GW announced US pipeline.
entries.thesisLong:
Eaton sits at the grid-to-chip layer: medium-voltage switchgear, busway, PDUs and the electrical balance of plant that moves power from the substation to the GPU. It is a physical-delivery bottleneck rather than a technology one, and the Q2 2026 numbers show it tightening.

Data center organic revenue grew 65% in the second quarter against an underlying market growth rate of about 23%, and data center orders rose roughly 240% year over year. The twelve-month rolling average of Electrical Americas orders was up 41% organically, total backlog at the end of June was up 33% over June 2025, and total electrical backlog was up 43% year over year — visibility that now extends through the second half of 2026 and into 2027. Eaton raised organic growth guidance alongside the print.

The forward pipeline is larger than the backlog and slower to convert. The announced US data center pipeline has reached 307 gigawatts, equivalent to roughly fifteen years of construction at the 2025 build rate, and the majority of Eaton's data center backlog translates to 2028 and beyond. That is the honest shape of this bottleneck: the constraint is real, but the revenue recognition is long-dated, and announced pipelines are not orders.

The risks follow from that: hyperscaler capex digestion before the 2028 deliveries land, input cost inflation on copper and steel, and competitive intensity from European electrical peers chasing the same demand.

entries.name: Grid & Gas Turbine Power
entries.thesisShort: GE Vernova is a primary supplier of gas turbines and grid equipment, and its gas equipment backlog plus slot reservations grew from 100 GW to 116 GW in Q2 2026 with only about 10 GW of 2029-2030 slots left uncommitted.
entries.thesisLong:
GE Vernova is where the AI power story stops being about electrons and starts being about factory slots. Gas Power equipment backlog and slot reservation agreements grew from 100 GW to 116 GW during Q2 2026, and the company now anticipates reaching at least 125 GW by year-end 2026.

The scarcity is in the calendar. Entering the first quarter GE Vernova had roughly 10 GW of available 2029 production capacity; customers then pulled aggressively into 2030 because engineering, procurement and construction schedules made the later slot more useful than the earlier one. After that reshuffle, approximately 10 GW remains available across 2029 and 2030 combined. When the next available delivery window for a large gas turbine is four years out and nearly sold, the turbine — not the permit and not the gas — is the binding constraint on new firm generation.

Capacity is being added, but slowly relative to demand. The company remains on track for a 20 GW annual gas turbine output rate in Q3 2026, 24 GW in 2028, and is implementing actions to reach 30 GW in 2030. Each of those steps requires forgings, castings and grain-oriented electrical steel from supply chains with their own multi-year lead times.

The risks are execution-shaped rather than demand-shaped: slot reservations are not firm orders until they convert, the long-lead supply chain gates the output ramp, the wind segment remains a drag on consolidated results, and utility capex is exposed to regulatory shifts.

entries.name: AI Server Integration
entries.thesisShort: Super Micro is the highest-velocity AI server integrator; fiscal 2026 revenue reached $39.1B, it booked over $60B of new orders in the June quarter, and it guided fiscal 2027 to $65-72B.
entries.thesisLong:
Super Micro is the highest-velocity AI server integrator — rack-scale liquid-cooled platforms shipped to hyperscalers, neoclouds and sovereign customers on cycle times its larger competitors do not match.

Fiscal 2026, ended 30 June 2026, was a step-change: revenue of $39.1B against $22.0B in fiscal 2025, at a full-year gross margin of 10.8%. The fourth quarter carried the acceleration — $11.1B of net sales versus $10.2B in Q3 and $5.8B a year earlier, with gross margin of 17.5% against 9.9% the prior quarter and 9.5% a year earlier, and net income of $1,178M versus $195M in Q4 FY2025. Margin expansion of that magnitude at this company is the single most notable line in the print, because thin margins have historically been the whole bear case.

The order book is what drives the forward guide. Super Micro received over $60B in new orders during the June quarter, taking the order book and backlog to record levels entering fiscal 2027, and guided the September quarter to $14.5-15.5B against roughly $11.7B of prior consensus, with full fiscal 2027 revenue of $65-72B against roughly $54.4B of consensus.

That gap between guidance and consensus is the risk as much as the opportunity. Guiding to nearly double fiscal 2026 revenue raises the execution bar on supply allocation, working capital and component pricing simultaneously, and customer concentration means a single large program slipping moves the whole year.
catalysts: Fiscal 2027 revenue guided to $65-72B on a record order book
Rubin-generation rack platforms shipping through fiscal 2027
Gross margin sustaining above the 10.8% FY2026 average
Sovereign AI customer wins
risks: Guidance far above prior consensus raises the execution bar
Historically thin gross margins under price competition
Customer concentration — one large program slipping moves the year
Working capital intensity funding a near-doubling of revenue

entries.name: AI Cluster Ethernet Switching
entries.thesisShort: Arista leads high-speed data center Ethernet switching for AI fabrics; Q2 2026 was its first $3B quarter, and it raised 2026 guidance to roughly $12.6B with an AI Fabrics target of at least $3.5B.
entries.thesisLong:
Arista is the leader in high-speed data center Ethernet switching and the named partner for hyperscaler AI fabrics. Q2 2026 was its first $3B quarter — revenue of $3.036B, up 37.7% year over year and above guidance — driven by both AI and enterprise demand.

Management raised the 2026 outlook to roughly 40% revenue growth, about $12.6B, lifted the operating margin target to 48-49% and held gross margin at 62-64%. The AI-specific target is at least $3.5B of AI Fabrics revenue for 2026, and Etherlink AI-fabric deployments now span more than 100 cumulative customers — a meaningful broadening from the handful of mega-scale accounts that defined the early AI networking cycle.

The most important detail from the quarter is the supply framing: AI networking demand remains materially above available supply. That inverts the usual read on a networking vendor's numbers. Revenue is not measuring demand, it is measuring what could be built and shipped, which is exactly what makes this a bottleneck rather than a share story. Scale-across networking — connecting AI clusters to each other rather than within a rack — is the newer vector, and could represent roughly 30% of the AI target.

The risks are concentration in a small number of very large customers, white-box and merchant-silicon adoption pressure at the low end, and renewed competition from Cisco in AI-specific designs.
catalysts: AI Fabrics revenue tracking to the ≥$3.5B 2026 target
Scale-across networking becoming a growing share of the AI target
1.6T fabric transition
Enterprise AI campus and inference deployments broadening the customer base
risks: AI networking demand above available supply — supply, not demand, caps realized revenue
Customer concentration in a small number of hyperscalers
White-box and merchant-silicon adoption pressure
Cisco competition in AI-specific designs

entries.name: Optical Transceivers & Lasers
entries.thesisShort: Coherent supplies the 800G and 1.6T optical transceivers that AI fabrics depend on; fiscal Q4 2026 was its first $2B quarter, with Datacenter & Communications at 79% of revenue and up 59% year over year.
entries.thesisLong:
Coherent sits at the optical interconnect layer, where the constraint is laser supply and transceiver manufacturing rather than switch silicon. Fiscal Q4 2026 was a record and the company's first $2B quarter: revenue of $2.05B, up 34% year over year, taking full-year FY2026 revenue to $7.12B, up 22.5%.

The mix shift is the story. Datacenter & Communications drove 79% of quarterly revenue and grew 59% year over year, supported by demand for both 800G and 1.6T transceivers. Co-packaged optics — where the optical engine moves onto the switch package rather than sitting in a pluggable module — is described as approaching revenue, which would be the first structural change to transceiver economics in several product generations.

The concentration that comes with that mix is the corresponding exposure. At 79% of revenue, datacom is no longer a segment inside a diversified photonics company; it is the company, and the non-datacom businesses no longer provide much counter-cyclical ballast. Pricing pressure from Asian transceiver competitors is the persistent structural risk in this category, and it bites hardest exactly when volume is scaling.
catalysts: 1.6T transceiver volume ramp
Co-packaged optics moving to revenue
Datacom mix continuing to lift consolidated growth
risks: Asian transceiver competition and pricing pressure
Concentration — datacom is now 79% of revenue
Cyclicality in the smaller non-datacom segments

entries.name: Optical Contract Manufacturing
entries.thesisShort: Fabrinet manufactures much of the high-speed optical transceiver supply chain; fiscal Q4 2026 revenue rose 45% to $1.316B with data center revenue up 68% to $669M.
entries.thesisLong:
Fabrinet is the contract manufacturer behind much of the high-speed optical supply chain — the company that physically builds transceivers and optical engines for the brands that sell them. Fiscal Q4 2026 revenue was $1.316B, up 45% year over year and above the high end of guidance, on broad-based strength across data center, communications infrastructure and automotive/industrial.

Data center is now the engine: $669M in the quarter, up 68% year over year, led by DCI products reaching a $1B annualized run rate alongside strong HPC growth. The forward shape is unusually legible for a contract manufacturer, because Fabrinet described the specific programs coming: a hyperscaler-direct transceiver program starting to ramp in the current quarter, a merchant program beginning in the December 2026 quarter, and further programs getting off the ground in early calendar 2027.

That sequencing is what makes Fabrinet a useful read on the optical bottleneck — it books the manufacturing slots before the transceivers appear in anyone's revenue. The exposures are the standard contract-manufacturing set: customer concentration, transceiver pricing commoditization as volumes scale, and geographic concentration in Thailand.

entries.name: EDA Software & IP
entries.thesisShort: Synopsys pairs EDA leadership with the broadest silicon IP portfolio and now Ansys multiphysics; Q2 FY2026 revenue rose 42% to $2.3B with Ansys contributing $652M.
entries.thesisLong:
Synopsys is one half of the EDA duopoly, and every leading-edge AI chip is designed with its tools and increasingly built from its IP. The Ansys acquisition — roughly $35B — changed the shape of the company from EDA-plus-IP to what management calls silicon-to-systems, pairing chip design with multiphysics simulation and analysis.

Q2 FY2026 showed the combination working through the P&L. Revenue rose 42% to $2.3B, with Design Automation revenue up 62% to $1.8B and Ansys contributing $652M. Synopsys Multiphysics Fusion integrates Ansys signoff engines directly with the EDA flow, which is the technical basis for the claim that a combined stack closes designs materially faster than stitching two vendors' tools together — and the specific axis on which Synopsys is now competing with Cadence.

Integration has had a visible cost. Roughly 2,000 employees, about 10% of the combined workforce, were cut post-merger. The other structural drag is policy: US export controls effectively restricted advanced EDA tools to Chinese customers across 2025-2026, removing a slice of historical revenue that all three major EDA vendors reported against.

The bottleneck logic is unchanged by any of this. There is no path to a leading-edge AI accelerator that routes around the two EDA houses, and the IP attach makes Synopsys content per design higher on each successive node.

chokepointMetrics.value: ~2,000 roles, about 10% of the combined workforce (2026)

Synopsys.ai monetization across the design flow
IP attach to AI accelerator designs
Restructuring benefits flowing through the P&L
risks: Renewed China export restrictions — the May 2025 EDA licensing requirement was rescinded in July 2025, leaving policy a live swing factor on roughly 16% of revenue rather than a booked loss
Ansys integration execution
Cadence competitive intensity

entries.name: EDA & System Design
entries.thesisShort: Cadence is Synopsys's twin in the EDA duopoly, with a dominant emulation business used for pre-silicon verification; Q2 2026 backlog reached a record $8.1B, up 27% year over year.
entries.thesisLong:
Cadence is the other half of the EDA duopoly, and its emulation and prototyping business is the specific chokepoint: every advanced AI chip is verified pre-silicon on hardware emulators before a mask set is committed, and there are very few credible suppliers of that hardware.

Q2 2026 beat across the guidance range. Revenue was $1.584B against $1.275B a year earlier, with non-GAAP diluted EPS of $2.11 versus $1.65. The line that matters most for a subscription-and-hardware business is backlog: $8.1B at quarter end, up 27% year over year, with $4.2B of remaining performance obligations expected to convert to revenue within twelve months. That is the visibility that lets Cadence raise a full-year guide with two quarters still to run.

Management raised 2026 guidance to 19% revenue growth — implying $6.26-6.34B — with non-GAAP operating margin of 44.25%, non-GAAP EPS of $8.10 and roughly $2B of operating cash flow at the midpoint, citing accelerating demand for AI-driven design solutions.

The risks are policy and competition. US export controls on advanced EDA tools to Chinese customers removed a slice of the historical revenue base across 2025-2026, and the Synopsys-Ansys combination now competes with Cadence across a wider silicon-to-systems surface than pure-play EDA ever did.
catalysts: $8.1B backlog converting through 2027
Cadence.AI monetization across the design flow
Multiphysics and system analysis expansion
IP attach to AI accelerator designs
risks: Renewed China export restrictions — the May 2025 EDA licensing requirement was rescinded in July 2025, leaving policy a live swing factor on roughly 12% of revenue
Synopsys-Ansys combination competing across silicon-to-systems
Renewal timing concentration in a backlog-driven model

entries.name: Nuclear Power for AI
entries.thesisShort: Constellation owns the largest US nuclear fleet and is restarting the former Three Mile Island Unit 1 — now the Crane Clean Energy Center — for Microsoft, with restart on track for 2027 and fuel on site by end-2026.
entries.thesisLong:
Constellation owns the largest US nuclear fleet and, following the $16.4B Calpine acquisition that closed in 2026, is the largest private power producer globally. Q2 2026 was its first full quarter post-acquisition: revenue rose 64% to $11B, adjusted operating earnings were $2.74 per share, nuclear output reached 44,666 gigawatt-hours, and the company held its 2026 outlook of $11-12 per share.

The headline asset is the restart of the former Three Mile Island Unit 1, now renamed the Christopher M. Crane Clean Energy Center, under a twenty-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft. Restart remains on track for 2027 following a FERC waiver from PJM interconnection rules granted on 1 June 2026, and the plant is on schedule to receive nuclear material by the end of 2026, to be held in storage pending approval to return to operations. Environmental review and public comment progressed through July 2026.

The complication is transmission rather than the reactor. PJM determined that transmission upgrades are needed to safely deliver all of the 835 MW unit's output to the grid — a reminder that in this cycle, restarting generation is often easier than moving it. The restart itself carries a roughly $1.6B price tag.

The broader chokepoint logic holds: existing, licensed, already-interconnected nuclear capacity is the scarcest firm clean power available on a data center's timeline, and Constellation owns more of it than anyone else. FERC rulings on co-location, operational incidents and power market volatility remain the live risks.

entries.name: Merchant Power & Texas Load Growth
entries.thesisShort: Vistra pairs a large nuclear fleet with Texas gas generation at the centre of AI load growth, and has now signed roughly 3.8 GW of twenty-year nuclear PPAs with AWS and Meta.
entries.thesisLong:
Vistra owns one of the largest US nuclear fleets alongside a substantial gas portfolio in Texas — the intersection of firm clean power and the fastest-growing data center load in the country. Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA was $1.767B, up 30% year over year from $1.35B, with Generation EBITDA up 68% to $994M and Retail roughly flat at $773M.

The contracting is what changes the business. Vistra has signed twenty-year nuclear PPAs totalling approximately 3.8 GW: 1,200 MW at Comanche Peak with AWS, with deliveries starting in Q4 2027, and 2,609 MW across its PJM plants with Meta. Combined with retail, those contracts are expected to shift close to 50% of EBITDA to retail and contracted sources, materially reducing merchant exposure. Comanche Peak is targeted for energization at the end of 2027. The company also unveiled a $1B Helix data center partnership with KKR and NVIDIA.

The honest caveat on all of it is timing. The largest contracted volumes do not start delivering until late 2027, so the EBITDA mix shift is announced rather than realized, and the intervening years remain merchant-exposed. Texas has also begun auditing its data center interconnection queue, though Vistra has indicated the baseload Comanche Peak project is not expected to be affected.

The residual risks are the ones that have always applied to merchant generation: power price volatility, weather tail risk in ERCOT, and gas commodity exposure.

entries.name: Small Modular Reactors
entries.thesisShort: Oklo is the highest-profile US advanced reactor developer, and in August 2026 its Groves isotope test reactor in Texas reached first criticality in about eleven months — though the commercial Aurora powerhouses remain years out.
entries.thesisLong:
Oklo is the highest-profile US advanced reactor developer aimed at powering data centers behind the meter, and 2026 gave it the first hard proof point the sector has been waiting for.

On 5 August 2026, Oklo's Groves isotope test reactor at Lockhart, Texas reached first criticality — roughly eleven months from greenfield, with substantial construction completed in 229 days, funded privately and sited privately under DOE oversight. Management describes it as the fastest greenfield-to-criticality transition for a full-scale privately funded reactor. Whatever weight one puts on the record framing, it converts Oklo from a licensing story into a company that has actually built and started a reactor.

The commercial fleet is a separate and slower timeline, and the distinction matters. Groves is an isotope test reactor, not an Aurora powerhouse. Aurora-INL is now targeted for 2028 startup, moved back from earlier late-2027 guidance, and the 1.2 GW Ohio campus supporting Meta is not expected online until around 2030. DOE approved the Nuclear Safety Design Agreement for Aurora-INL early in 2026 and the Preliminary Documented Safety Analysis on 11 June 2026, and Oklo has completed two of four steps for DOE authorisation to fabricate its initial core at the Aurora Fuel Fabrication Facility at INL, drawing on 5 metric tons of HALEU allocated under a 2019 INL cooperative agreement plus EBR-II recovered fuel.

The pipeline is large and soft: approximately 14 GW of non-binding letters of intent, including a 12 GW arrangement with data center operator Switch and an LOI with Equinix. Oklo ended Q2 2026 with $3.0B of cash and marketable securities against a $124.2M first-half loss from operations, so funding is not the near-term constraint — conversion and construction are.

entries.name: Uranium Mining & Fuel Cycle
entries.thesisShort: Cameco is the largest Western uranium miner and, via its 49% Westinghouse stake, sits inside the largest non-Russian fuel-cycle franchise — now attached to an $80B US government reactor programme.
entries.thesisLong:
Cameco is the largest Western uranium miner and, through its 49% stake in Westinghouse (Brookfield holds 51%), sits inside the largest non-Russian fuel-cycle and reactor franchise. The commodity is the input to every nuclear plant powering AI load, and the fuel cycle is where Western supply is thinnest.

Q2 2026, reported on 31 July, was a softer quarter operationally: net earnings of $25M and adjusted EBITDA of $391M, taking first-half figures to $156M and $899M respectively. The year-over-year decline came mainly from lower equity earnings at Westinghouse and lower planned sales volumes, partly offset by higher average realized prices in both uranium and fuel services. Cameco reaffirmed 2026 uranium production guidance of 19.5-21.5 million pounds despite flooding-related disruption at its northern Saskatchewan operations.

The Westinghouse leg is where the AI linkage is most direct. The US government, Brookfield, Cameco and Westinghouse announced an $80B strategic partnership to deploy AP1000 reactors explicitly framed against data center electricity demand, backed by $17.5B in DOE loan facilities, with Westinghouse stating in July 2026 that it plans ten new US plants with construction starting in 2030. Westinghouse also confidentially submitted a draft Form S-1 to the SEC on 31 July 2026 for a proposed IPO, which would put a public market value on an asset currently carried through equity accounting.

Spot uranium traded near $86.5 per pound in early August 2026 and has been range-bound, while long-term contract pricing has moved to multi-year highs on structural supply deficits — the divergence that matters most for a producer whose book is largely long-term contracted.
